source_text: As President Donald Trump’s approval rating plunges to a historic low of 36 percent, experts have an increasingly dismal assessment of his second administration. “This is what a crater looks like in politics,” said pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher . “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.” Trump’s approval rating was already low, but his latest drop is among the sharpest declines of either of his terms. It comes as he confronts a series of crises largely of his own making. The first is the economy. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked the economy as their top concern — its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. Cost of living skyrocketed in the wake of COVID-19, and while then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and rebounded the economy faster than any other nation , a financially rattled electorate voted for Trump thinking his economic approach would outperform that of Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden. But voter hopes haven’t panned out. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer. Trump hasn’t exactly delivered on that, famously making obtuse statements like “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30 ” as the economy soured under the weight of his tariffs. What’s more, the fact that gas prices are approaching record highs not only says something about the Trump economy, but links to the second major reason Americans are displeased with the president: his war on Iran. Just 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week ago. Only 26 percent agree with Trump’s assertion that the war will make the U.S. safer, and a mere 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground. And with gas prices spiking up to a national average just shy of $4 and no clear end in sight to the war, Americans are not happy with how Trump’s military “excursion” is hurting them at the pump. Trump may dismiss concerns over affordability as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters aren’t buying it.

source_text:
As President Donald Trump’s approval rating plunges to a historic low of 36 percent, experts are offering an increasingly grim assessment of a second administration defined by economic hardship, militarism, and policy choices that have intensified insecurity for ordinary people. “This is what a crater looks like in politics,” said pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher. “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.”

Trump’s approval rating was already low, but the latest drop ranks among the sharpest declines of either of his terms. It comes as he confronts a series of crises largely created by his own administration. The first is the economy. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked the economy as their top concern — its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. The cost of living skyrocketed in the wake of COVID-19, and while then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and saw the economy rebound faster than that of any other nation, a financially battered electorate voted for Trump, believing his economic approach would outperform that of Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden’s policies.

Those hopes have not materialized. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer. But Trump has not delivered meaningful relief, instead making dismissive statements such as “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30” as tariffs increased economic pressure on families already struggling with rising costs.

The fact that gas prices are approaching record highs further exposes the consequences of Trump’s economic agenda and connects to the second major reason Americans are dissatisfied with him: his war on Iran. Just 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week ago. Only 26 percent agree with Trump’s assertion that the war will make the United States safer, and a mere 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground. With gas prices spiking to a national average just shy of $4 and no clear end in sight to the war, Americans are paying for Trump’s military “excursion” at the pump while broader social needs remain unmet.

Trump may dismiss concerns over affordability as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters are rejecting that denial.

source_text: Another cinema in Singapore is closing... but the big screen isn’t gone yet Golden Village has announced that its Tiong Bahru Plaza outlet will close at the end of March 2026 after more than 30 years in operation, making it one of the oldest cinemas in Singapore to shut in recent years. The closure adds to a growing list of theatres that have disappeared, including Shaw Seletar, Cathay Cineplexes locations, and The Projector’s former Golden Mile venue, as the movie-going scene continues to change with streaming platforms and shifting audience habits. Still, new operators like Filmhouse taking over The Projector and the presence of around 30 cinema locations islandwide show that the big screen experience isn’t gone yet, even if it doesn’t look the same as before. #8dayssg #8dayssgtrending #singapore #sgnews #cinema

rewritten_text:
Softcare’s revenue rose by 25% last year and its profit increased by 27%, as its focus on consumers in emerging markets produced strong results. Image credit: Bamboo Works.

Softcare reported 25% revenue growth last year, driven by a 134% increase in Latin America and double-digit growth across its core African markets. The results place the diaper maker at the forefront of a new wave of Chinese companies pursuing consumers in Africa and other emerging markets.

Known as the “African diaper king,” Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) has defied skeptics who questioned whether it could maintain its dominant position in Africa, as well as expand successfully into other emerging markets. Investors responded positively to the company’s first annual results after its IPO late last week, pushing its shares up nearly 15% over the two trading days following the announcement.

The company’s revenue rose 24.9% year over year to $567 million last year, while net profit increased 27.4% to $121 million. Its gross profit margin also rose from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025.

Sales in its core African markets increased 22.5% to $545 million. Softcare is also expanding beyond Africa, seeking growth among consumers in other emerging markets. Latin America is the clearest example: sales there more than doubled to $22 million, just five years after the company entered Peru in 2020 and added El Salvador in 2024.

The company is also building a presence in Central Asia, where sales remain small but more than doubled last year to $272,000.

After several years of declines, average selling prices for Softcare’s two largest product lines rose between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper prices increased 4.4% year over year, with that segment accounting for 78.6% of total revenue. Prices for feminine hygiene products rose 7%, representing 17.5% of revenue.

These increases matter because they indicate that Softcare is persuading consumers in highly price-sensitive markets to pay more for essential products, allowing the company to preserve and even improve its margins. For households facing financial pressures, however, higher prices also underscore the tension between corporate profitability and access to basic hygiene goods.

In a previous prospectus issued before its November IPO last year, the company reported that profit growth had slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024, down from explosive 252% growth in 2023. A later filing showed that profit growth slowed further, to just 12% in the first four months ... Full story available on Benzinga.com

source_text: The Competition Commission of India has approved the proposed consolidation of online education companies, clearing the way for Coursera’s subsidiary, Chess Merger Sub, to merge with Udemy Inc. The all-stock transaction, valued at approximately USD 2.5 billion, will place Udemy under Coursera’s full ownership. Existing Coursera shareholders will control about 59% of the combined entity, while Udemy stockholders will hold 41%, marking further concentration of ownership and decision-making in the online education sector.

source_text: Delhi PWD Accelerates PNG Pipeline Laying with 24-Hour Approvals In a bid to expedite infrastructure development for cleaner fuel access, the Delhi Public Works Department (PWD) has announced a significant policy shift. Effective immediately, road-cutting permissions for laying PNG pipelines by Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL) will be approved within 24 hours of receiving a complete request. The department, responsible for overseeing the capital's road infrastructure, has also waived road restoration charges for the next three months until June 30, 2026. This move aims to accelerate the installation of PNG connections by removing financial and bureaucratic hurdles. Officials emphasized that IGL is expected to prioritize this task, ensuring swift work completion supported by adequate manpower. Additionally, the areas excavated during pipeline installation must be backfilled securely to avoid public hazards. This initiative highlights the government's commitment to improving public access to cleaner energy in Delhi.

The department, which oversees Delhi’s road infrastructure, has also waived road restoration charges for three months, through June 30, 2026. The measure is intended to accelerate PNG connections and make infrastructure expansion more accessible by reducing delays and costs.

Officials said IGL is expected to treat the work as a priority and complete it quickly with adequate manpower. They also stressed that excavated areas must be securely backfilled to prevent hazards for the public. The initiative reflects the government’s stated commitment to expanding public access to cleaner energy while requiring responsible implementation and protection of residents using the city’s roads.
